# 3.1 Thinking in Components & JSX Rules ## What is React? React is a JavaScript library for building user interfaces from reusable components. Think about a page like this: ```text Page ├── Header ├── Sidebar ├── CourseCard ├── CourseCard └── Footer ``` Each piece can become a component. A component is usually a JavaScript function that returns JSX. ```jsx function Welcome() { return

Strings vs JavaScript expressions Quoted JSX attribute: ```jsx ``` This is a literal string. Dynamic value: ```jsx const imageUrl = "/avatar.png"; ``` The curly braces mean: > "Evaluate JavaScript here." --- ## 7. Numbers and booleans Use curly braces for non-string values. ```jsx ``` This is different from: ```jsx ``` The first passes a number and boolean. The second passes strings. --- ## 8. Conditional rendering You can use ordinary JavaScript: ```jsx function Status({ online }) { if (online) { return

"Logout" : "Login"} ``` A statement such as a full `if` block cannot usually be dropped directly inside JSX. topics.title: 3.2 Props & Unidirectional Data Flow
topics.description: Pass dynamic data and callback functions from parent components to child components.
topics.lessonMarkdown:
# 3.2 Props & Unidirectional Data Flow ## What are props? Props are information passed from a parent component to a child component. Imagine a function call: ```javascript greet("Anu"); ``` A React component works similarly: ```jsx ``` The child receives a `name` prop. --- ## 1. The simplest prop ```jsx function Greeting({ name }) { return

Hello, {name}!

; } export default function App() { return ; } ``` The parent provides the data. The child reads the data. --- ## 2. Props can be many JavaScript types String: ```jsx ``` Number: ```jsx ``` Boolean: ```jsx ``` Object: ```jsx ``` Array: ```jsx ``` Function: ```jsx ``` Even JSX: ```jsx

Hello

 ``` --- ## 3. Destructuring props Instead of: ```jsx function UserCard(props) { return

{props.user.name}

; } ``` you can write: ```jsx function UserCard({ user }) { return

{user.name}

; } ``` You can destructure multiple values: ```jsx function ProductCard({ title, price, inStock }) { return (

{title}

${price}

{inStock ? "In stock" : "Out of stock"}
); } ``` --- ## 4. Props are read-only A child should not modify the parent's props. Do not do: ```javascript props.name = "Changed"; // ❌ ``` If the UI needs to change, the parent usually owns the state and passes a callback. --- ## 5. Data flows down React generally follows one-way data flow: ```text Parent state ↓ props ↓ Child component ``` For example: ```jsx function Parent() { const [status, setStatus] = useState("Standby"); return ( setStatus("Online")} /> ); } ``` The parent owns the state. The child receives the callback. --- ## 6. Child-to-parent communication Children don't directly edit parent state. Instead: ```jsx function ActionButton({ onAction }) { return ( ); } ``` Parent: ```jsx setStatus("Online")} /> ``` The child says: > "The user clicked." The parent decides: > "Update the application state." This is a very important architecture pattern. --- ## 7. Default prop values You can provide a fallback: ```jsx function Avatar({ size = 48 }) { return ; } ``` When no size is supplied, `48` is used. --- ## 8. Props are snapshots Think of props as the values a component receives for a particular render. If the parent changes state: ```text parent state changes ↓ parent renders again ↓ new props ↓ child renders with new values ``` This is why props can appear to "change", even though the child should not mutate them. --- ## Example: reusable button ```jsx function ActionButton({ label, onAction }) { return ( ); } function App() { const [status, setStatus] = useState("Standby"); return (

{status}

setStatus("Online")} />
); } ``` This is the same pattern used by reusable buttons, cards, dialogs, tables, forms, and navigation components. --- ## 9. The exercise connection Your exercise contains: ```jsx function ActionButton({ label, onAction }) { return ( ); } ``` The parent uses: ```jsx setStatus("Online")} /> ``` So: ```text Parent owns state ↓ passes label + callback ↓ ActionButton ↓ user clicks ↓ callback runs ↓ parent changes state ↓ UI updates ``` --- ## Common mistakes ### Passing a function incorrectly Wrong: ```jsx onClick={onAction()} ``` Right: ```jsx onClick={onAction} ``` ### Passing string instead of number ```jsx ``` passes a string. ```jsx ``` passes a number. ### Mutating props Never treat props as your own mutable storage. --- ## Mini challenge What will render? ```jsx function Greeting({ name = "Learner" }) { return

Hello {name}

; } ``` Output: ```text Hello Learner Hello Anu ``` Further reading: - React: Passing Props to a Component — https://react.dev/learn/passing-props-to-a-component - React: Describing the UI — https://react.dev/learn/describing-the-ui - Scrimba: React introduction — https://docs.scrimba.com/react/introduction - GeeksforGeeks: Props in React — https://www.geeksforgeeks.org/reactjs/what-are-props-in-react/

topics.title: 3.3 Multi-File Architecture & Component Extraction
topics.description: Learn real-world React folder structure by breaking monolithic code into modular component files in src/components/ with relative imports.

codeStudio.title: Component Separation & Folder Architecture
codeStudio.description:
Learn how a real React project is divided into files. Start with a single App component, identify repeated UI, extract it into src/components/, export it, import it, and finally render multiple instances with props.

Before editing, understand this mental model:
src/App.jsx → imports → src/components/Header.jsx
                   └──────→ src/components/ProfileCard.jsx

Relative paths begin with './' when the target is inside the current folder. A default export can be imported with any local name, but keeping the same component name is the clearest convention.
